text.p: German defence and engineering group Rheinmetall AG said on Tuesday it paid an at-market price of around 900 million marks to raise its stake in auto parts maker Kolbenschmidt AG to a controlling 53.5 percent.
Rheinmetall said it bought 28.5 percent of Kolbenschmidt through a group of banks, adding to a 25 percent holding it had earlier acquired from Commerzbank AG and on the German stock market.

A company spokesman gave no details on the timing of the purchase but at Monday's closing price for Kolbenschmidt shares on the Frankfurt stock exchange of 33.90 marks, the stake would be valued at 912 million marks.
He told Reuters the purchase price was "oriented towards" the market price for Kolbenschmidt stock but declined to give details of how the purchase was financed.
The takeover marks the end of a months-long courtship by Rheinmetall, during which it was challenged for control of Kolbenschmidt by Britain's T&N.

"Rheinmetall has fulfilled its publicly announced intention to integrate Kolbenschmidt into its business, thereby meeting the expectations of the financial community," the company said in a statement.

T&N, which had held an option to buy a quarter stake in Kolbenschmidt from investors, had no immediate comment. But it had said last month that it wanted to keep a minority 12 percent stake in Kolbenschmidt after a Rheinmetall takeover.
The takeover, already cleared by the German cartel office, was given a cautious welcome by industry analysts.
They said the planned merger of Kolbenschmidt with Rheinmetall's Pierburg AG automotive unit would create some synergy potential.
"I think Rheinmetall has paid a fair price -- but it's not as cheap as it was a couple of months ago," said Rolla Kautz, auto analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
The deal, she said, would offer some possibilities to build more integrated car engine systems, rather than offering separate components as the the two companies now do.
Juergen Pieper at Deutsche Bank Research said the timing of the move, after two years of profits following a string of heavy losses at Kolbenschmidt, was good.
But, although there would be room for cost savings at the administrative and purchasing levels, he saw less synergy potential at the product level.
"Any share price potential for Kolbenschmidt is exhausted from my point of view at current levels," Pieper said.
Werner Friedmann, who follows Rheinmetall for Bank Julius Baer, also said the critical mass created by the takeover would help. "Size is not a hindrance," he said.

But he saw no reason to change his "market performer" rating for Rheinmetall after a recent acquisition spree by the Duesseldorf-based group, which has included buys in the defence electronics sector of STN Atlas and Richard Hirschmann.
Rheinmetall stock closed on the Frankfurt bourse down three marks to 390 marks -- but only after opening at a year-high of 395 marks. Kolbenschmidt closed up 40 pfennigs at 34.30 marks.

Rheinmetall said the merger would create its largest business area in terms of sales. Taken together, Kolbenschmidt and Pierburg employ over 10,000 workers and have combined sales of 2.3 billion marks.
Adding the automotive electronics operations of Hirschmann and Preh, another Rheinmetall unit, the group's auto business should turn over three billion marks this year.
Despite a likely delay to the execution of the deal, an extraordinary shareholders meeting will be called this year by Kolbenschmidt to clear the takeover.
Rheinmetall will then own over 75 percent of a merged unit made up of Kolbenschmidt and Pierburg, and will consolidate the subsidiary's results into its 1997 accounts.
